l: land of Canaan, The Book of Joshua
s: The land of Canaan is the territory the LORD gave the children of Israel, as sworn to their fathers. It was subdued before Israel, and its inheritances were distributed by lot, with the Levites receiving only cities. The remaining tribes' portions were surveyed in seven parts, while Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh held land east of the Jordan. The land came to rest from war, and Israel possessed and lived in it, fulfilling the promise.

l: ark of the covenant, The Book of Joshua
s: The ark of the covenant is the LORD's own covenant ark, called the ark of the Lord of all the earth and owned by the LORD. Levitical priests carry it ahead of the people, who follow it to learn the way. At the Jordan, its passing cuts off the waters; it rests on dry ground mid-river until the whole nation crosses, then crosses itself, prompting the memorial stones. Later, priests bear it in procession around Jericho, with armed men before and a rear guard after, circling once daily for six days and seven times on the seventh.

l: Levitical priests, The Book of Joshua
s: The Levitical priests are a group who bear the LORD's ark of the covenant. At Joshua's command they lead the people into the Jordan, where the waters are cut off at their feet. They stand firm on dry ground until all Israel has crossed, then come up, and the waters return.

l: Canaanites, The Book of Joshua
s: The Canaanites are a group who remained in the land despite Israelite tribes' efforts. In Gezer they were not driven out by Ephraim and became servants in forced labor. In Manasseh's allotment they held cities such as Beth Shean and Megiddo. Once Israel grew strong they were subjected to forced labor, not expelled. Valley Canaanites had iron chariots, yet Joshua said they would be driven out.

l: Jebusites, The Book of Joshua
s: inhabit Jerusalem [Judah could not drive them out] The Jebusites are the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and Judah's northern border passes by the side of the Jebusite city. The children of Judah could not drive them out, and they live with the children of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.

l: crossing of the Jordan, The Book of Joshua
s: occurs_near Jericho The crossing takes place after three days of camping, with the priests bearing the ark going first into the overflowing Jordan. The waters stop and rise in one heap at Adam, and the people pass over near Jericho on dry ground. The priests stand firm in the riverbed until the whole nation has passed completely over.

l: twelve stones, The Book of Joshua
s: Twelve memorial stones, one per tribe, were taken by twelve men from the Jordan's middle and carried to camp, then set up by Joshua at Gilgal to answer future children's questions. Joshua also set twelve stones in the Jordan where the priests stood.

l: Gilgal, The Book of Joshua
s: Gilgal is a place on the east border of Jericho, in the plains of Jericho, where Israel encamped after crossing the Jordan. Joshua set up twelve river stones there as a memorial for future generations. Passover was kept there. It received its name when the LORD said he had rolled away the reproach of Egypt, a name said to endure.

l: circumcision, The Book of Joshua
s: Circumcision was neglected for children born in the wilderness on the journey. In Chapter 5 the LORD commands Joshua to circumcise Israel's sons again with flint knives; he does so, the people rest in camp until healed, and the reproach of Egypt is rolled away.

l: generation of the exodus (men of war who came out of Egypt), The Book of Joshua
s: The generation of men of war who left Egypt were all circumcised, yet disobeyed the LORD by not heeding his voice. They were consumed in the wilderness over forty years, and the LORD swore they would not see the promised land; their children replaced them.

l: commander of the LORD's army, The Book of Joshua
s: is_called prince of the LORD's army A man stands before Joshua near Jericho with his sword drawn and answers Joshua's question with "No," saying he has come as commander of the LORD's army. Joshua worships him, and he tells Joshua to take off his sandals because the place where he stands is holy.

l: priests (seven priests), The Book of Joshua
s: bear trumpets of rams’ horns [seven priests bear seven trumpets before the ark] Seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD and blow them as they march around Jericho. They do this once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh day. Their trumpet blast at the seventh circuit precedes Joshua's command to shout.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua
s: Israel, called the children of Israel, is a covenant people composed of tribes such as Judah and led by Joshua, elders, heads, judges and officers. It is bound to the LORD by covenant and obligated to keep the book of the law of Moses, holding fast to the LORD. Its land in Canaan, a good land stretching from the Jordan to the great sea, is a gift from the LORD, not something it labored for. The records open with Jericho: Israel marches as commanded, shouts at the trumpet, takes the city, and is warned against devoted things. Achan's trespass in taking them makes Israel itself devoted for destruction; it flees before Ai until Achan and his household are found by tribe, family and household, then stoned and burned. Israel then feigns defeat, takes Ai, and gathers at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal to hear the law. At Gibeon it fails to seek the LORD's counsel, is deceived, and spares the Gibeonites because of its oath. It defeats the Amorite coalition, conquers the south, then the northern coalition, and the land rests from war. Remaining peoples such as the Geshurites and Maacathites are not driven out and still live within Israel. The land is allotted by tribe, and Levites receive cities from Israel's inheritance. Israel enjoys rest on every side, with no enemy standing against it. In Joshua's charge, Israel is told to be courageous, keep the law, hold fast to the LORD, and not mingle with the remaining nations, on pain of perishing from the good land. At Shechem the assembled leaders hear the history of the LORD's deliverance, vow repeatedly to serve the LORD, call themselves witnesses against themselves, and agree to put away foreign gods. Israel serves the LORD throughout Joshua's lifetime and that of the elders who outlived him, and buries Joseph's bones at Shechem.

l: wall of Jericho, The Book of Joshua
s: is_in_state fallen flat [when the people shouted] The LORD says the city wall will fall down flat when the people shout at the long ram's horn blast. When the people shout on the seventh day, the wall falls down flat, and the people go up into the city, each man straight in front of him.

l: devoted things (Jericho's silver, gold, bronze, iron), The Book of Joshua
s: is_forbidden_to Israel [taking them is a covenant transgression] The devoted things were taken in part by Achan, which was a trespass and a breach of the LORD's covenant. The LORD said Israel had become devoted for destruction and he would not be with them unless the devoted things were destroyed from among them. The robe, silver, and gold were found hidden in Achan's tent and laid before the LORD.

l: destruction of Jericho, The Book of Joshua
s: has_method edge of the sword and fire [all living things killed, city burned] After the wall falls, the people utterly destroy everything in the city with the sword: man and woman, young and old, ox, sheep and donkey. The city and all in it are burned, except that the silver, gold, bronze and iron go into the treasury of the LORD's house. Only Rahab and her household are spared.

l: march around Jericho, The Book of Joshua
s: has_duration seven days [once daily for six days, seven times on the seventh] On six days the armed men, seven priests with trumpets and the ark circle the city once daily, then return to camp, while the people stay silent. On the seventh day they rise early and circle seven times, and at the final blast Joshua commands the shout. The march ends with the wall falling and the city being taken.

l: Achan, The Book of Joshua
s: Achan, son of Carmi and descendant of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took devoted things: a robe, silver, and gold, hiding them in his tent. Singled out by the LORD's selection, he confessed to Joshua, then was stoned and burned with his family, livestock, and possessions in the valley of Achor.

l: Ai, The Book of Joshua
s: Ai is a small city east of Bethel, beside Beth Aven, ruled by a king. Spies judged its people few, yet it routed about three thousand attacking Israelites, killing roughly thirty-six. Israel later returned, lured out the men of Ai and Bethel, and took the open city by ambush, burning it into a lasting desolate heap.

l: tribe of Judah, The Book of Joshua
s: The tribe of Judah is an Israelite group allotted land in the south, bounded by Edom, the wilderness of Zin and the great sea, with Caleb receiving a portion and its cities listed by region. It failed to drive the Jebusites from Jerusalem, who still live with it. Its portion proved too large, so part went to Simeon.

l: valley of Achor, The Book of Joshua
s: The valley of Achor is where Israel stoned and burned Achan, his family, and stolen goods; a heap of stones was raised over him, and the place, named 'trouble' for his sin, keeps that name today.

l: Achan's sin and judgment, The Book of Joshua
s: has_penalty burning with fire [for whoever is taken with the devoted thing] Achan's covetous taking of devoted plunder and hiding it in his tent brought the LORD's anger on all Israel. He was exposed by a selection through tribe, family, and household, confessed, and the hidden goods were recovered. He and all that he had were stoned and burned in the valley of Achor, and the LORD turned from his anger.

l: defeat at Ai, The Book of Joshua
s: Israel's defeat at Ai: about three thousand men, sent on the spies' advice, fled and thirty-six died. Hearts melted, Joshua and elders mourned, and the LORD blamed the devoted thing, Achan's sin.

l: king of Ai, The Book of Joshua
s: The king of Ai rushes out early with his people to fight Israel, unaware of the ambush behind his city. He is captured alive and brought to Joshua, hanged on a tree until evening, then buried under a heap of stones at the city gate.

l: men of Ai, The Book of Joshua
s: has_fate all killed [none remained or escaped] The men of Ai go out against Israel and pursue the fleeing Israelites away from their city, believing it is like the first time. They see the city's smoke behind them, are trapped between Israel's forces, and are struck down so that none remain or escape.

l: ambush force (Joshua's men at Ai), The Book of Joshua
s: Joshua's ambush force, stated as about five thousand men (elsewhere thirty thousand), hides west of Ai between Bethel and Ai by night, then rises when Joshua stretches out his javelin, enters the city, captures it and burns it.

l: Mount Ebal, The Book of Joshua
s: has_feature Joshua's altar Mount Ebal is where Joshua builds an altar to the LORD and writes a copy of Moses' law on stones. Half of the people stand in front of it, and half in front of Mount Gerizim, for the blessing and the reading of the law.

l: altar (Joshua's altar on Mount Ebal), The Book of Joshua
s: is_made_of uncut stones [no iron lifted on them] Joshua builds the altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, of uncut stones on which no one had lifted up any iron, as Moses commanded and as written in the book of the law. Israel offers burnt offerings and sacrifices peace offerings on it.

l: destruction of Ai, The Book of Joshua
s: has_death_toll twelve thousand [men and women] Ai is destroyed through the ambush and the feigned retreat, with twelve thousand men and women falling that day, and Joshua does not draw back his hand until all its inhabitants are utterly destroyed. The city is burned and made a permanent heap and desolation, its livestock and goods are taken as spoil, and its king is hanged and buried under stones at the gate.

l: Gibeonites, The Book of Joshua
s: The Gibeonites were Hivites living in Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim. Fearing for their lives after Joshua's victories at Jericho and Ai, they tricked Israel into a covenant. When exposed, they cited the LORD's command to Moses, submitted to Joshua's judgment, and were made wood cutters and drawers of water. Later, at peace with Israel, they appealed to Joshua at Gilgal as his servants, and he came with his army to rescue them.

l: princes of the congregation, The Book of Joshua
s: hold_position binding oath [refuse to touch the Gibeonites] The princes swear an oath to the Gibeonites by the LORD, the God of Israel. When the congregation murmurs, they insist the oath must be honored lest wrath fall on Israel, and they decree that the Gibeonites live as wood cutters and drawers of water.

l: covenant with the Gibeonites, The Book of Joshua
s: Joshua makes a peace covenant with the Gibeonites to let them live, and the princes swear an oath by the LORD. Its basis proves false, yet the oath is honored out of fear of wrath, sparing them.

l: Gibeonite deception, The Book of Joshua
s: The Gibeonites trick Israel by posing as distant travelers in worn clothing and moldy bread. Because Israel did not consult the LORD, a covenant is made; three days later their nearby home is discovered and Joshua confronts them.

l: Gibeon, The Book of Joshua
s: Gibeon is a great city, royal-city-like and larger than Ai, with mighty men and Hivite inhabitants who made peace with Israel. Five Amorite kings besieged it for that peace, and Joshua came and relieved it.

l: wood cutters and drawers of water, The Book of Joshua
s: serve LORD's altar This is the servile role assigned to the Gibeonites by the princes and then by Joshua, who makes them serve the congregation and the LORD's altar in the place he should choose. It is presented as a lasting condition that continues to this day, in place of killing them.

l: Adoni-Zedek, The Book of Joshua
s: Adoni-Zedek is the king of Jerusalem who, fearing Israel after Ai, Jericho and Gibeon's peace, rallied four kings against Gibeon, then hid with them in Makkedah's cave and was killed.

l: five Amorite kings, The Book of Joshua
s: Five Amorite kings, of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon, united to besiege Gibeon but were routed by Israel and the LORD. They hid in a cave at Makkedah, were brought out, humiliated, struck down, hanged on five trees, and thrown into the cave.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Joshua
s: Jerusalem, also called the Jebusite, appears in a boundary description where the border runs by the valley of Hinnom's son; Judah's children failed to expel its Jebusite inhabitants, who still live there.

l: Hebron, The Book of Joshua
s: Hebron is a city in the hill country of Judah, formerly called Kiriath Arba after the greatest man among the Anakim, described as the father of Anak. Joshua gave it to Caleb son of Jephunneh as an inheritance because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly, and it remained his to this day. Caleb drove out Anak's three sons from it. It appears in Judah's hill country list, in the group of nine, and serves as a city of refuge for the man slayer.

l: Makkedah, The Book of Joshua
s: has_status destroyed [taken by Joshua with its king] Makkedah was where the pursuit reached, and the five kings hid in a cave there. Joshua later took the city on that day, struck it and its king with the sword, and left no one remaining.

l: cave at Makkedah, The Book of Joshua
s: A cave at Makkedah where five Amorite kings hid; Joshua sealed it with stones and guards, then after their killing their bodies were thrown back in and the entrance resealed, stones remaining today.

l: hailstones, The Book of Joshua
s: Great stones sent by the LORD from the sky at Beth Horon's descent struck fleeing Amorites as far as Azekah, killing more than the Israelites' swords did.

l: sun and moon standing still, The Book of Joshua
s: Joshua commands the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Aijalon; they remain about a whole day until the nation avenges itself on its enemies. Recorded in the book of Jashar, unique: no day like it before or after.

l: Battle of Gibeon, The Book of Joshua
s: Israelite victory at Gibeon: after a night march from Gilgal, Joshua surprised five Amorite kings' armies; the LORD confused them, and the rout ran through Beth Horon to Makkedah, aided by hailstones and sun standing still.

l: Gezer, The Book of Joshua
s: inhabited_by Canaanites Gezer is named as a point on the border of the children of Joseph, after lower Beth Horon, before the border ends at the sea. Canaanites lived there and were not driven out by Ephraim, remaining in Ephraim's territory as forced laborers.

l: Debir, The Book of Joshua
s: Debir, formerly Kiriath Sepher and also called Kiriath Sannah, is a hill country city. Caleb offered Achsah to its conqueror, and Othniel took it. A Debir also appears in a border description near Achor.

l: Canaanite land conquered by Joshua, The Book of Joshua
s: The Canaanite land Joshua conquered spans the hill country, South, Goshen, lowland and Arabah, from Mount Halak to Baal Gad under Hermon. After he took all of it, he divided it among Israel's tribes as inheritance, and it rested from war.

l: Jabin, The Book of Joshua
s: Jabin, king of Hazor, rallies other kings into a coalition against Israel's conquests, but is struck down with the sword when Joshua takes Hazor.

l: Hazor, The Book of Joshua
s: has_status head of all those kingdoms [formerly] Hazor is described as formerly the head of all those kingdoms. Joshua takes it, kills its king and all its people, and burns it, the only city on a mound that Israel burned.

l: northern coalition of kings, The Book of Joshua
s: A northern coalition of kings, summoned by Jabin, unites Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite and other peoples with vast armies and many horses and chariots, but is routed and destroyed by Israel.

l: waters of Merom, The Book of Joshua
s: is_a encampment site of the kings [coalition camped there to fight Israel] The waters of Merom are where all the allied kings meet and encamp together to fight Israel. Joshua attacks them there suddenly.

l: Battle of Merom, The Book of Joshua
s: Joshua and all the warriors attack the encamped coalition at the waters of Merom, and the LORD delivers them into Israel's hand. Israel chases them to great Sidon, Misrephoth Maim and the valley of Mizpah, leaving none remaining, and then hamstrings the horses and burns the chariots.

l: Anakim, The Book of Joshua
s: The Anakim are a people Joshua cut off from the hill country, including Hebron, Debir, Anab, Judah and Israel, utterly destroying them and their cities; only Gaza, Gath and Ashdod retain a remnant.

l: utter destruction of the inhabitants, The Book of Joshua
s: commanded_by Moses [as commanded by the servant of the LORD] Israel strikes every person in Hazor and the other captured cities with the sword, leaving none who breathed, while taking the plunder and livestock. The text presents this as commanded by the LORD through Moses, and as the purpose of the LORD hardening the peoples' hearts so they would receive no favor.

l: kings of the land, The Book of Joshua
s: A group of thirty-one kings west of the Jordan, each ruling one city from Jericho and Ai to Tirzah across varied regions and peoples. They were defeated by Joshua and the Israelites; Moses and Israel had earlier defeated kings east of the Jordan.

l: tribe of Levi, The Book of Joshua
s: has_inheritance offerings of the LORD made by fire [instead of land] The tribe of Levi was given no land inheritance. Instead the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and the LORD, the God of Israel, himself, are its inheritance, as he spoke to them.

l: Canaan land remaining to be possessed, The Book of Joshua
s: Territory still unconquered in Canaan, listed by the LORD: Philistine and Geshurite regions, Canaanite land, Sidonian Mearah to Aphek, Gebalite land, and all Lebanon eastward to Hamath's entrance; the LORD will drive out hill-country inhabitants.

l: Transjordan inheritance, The Book of Joshua
s: Transjordan inheritance is the land east of the Jordan, including Gilead, Bashan to Salecah, and Mount Hermon. Moses had already distributed it to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, from the kingdoms of Sihon and Og, though Geshur and Maacath were not driven out. Canaan's lots, cast by Eleazar and Joshua for nine and a half tribes, followed; Levites received cities, and Caleb received Hebron.

l: Caleb the son of Jephunneh, The Book of Joshua
s: Caleb, a Kenizzite counted among the children of Judah, is a man who wholly followed the LORD. Sent at forty from Kadesh Barnea to spy out the land, he reported faithfully while his brothers disheartened the people, earning Moses' promise of the land he walked on. At eighty-five, kept alive by the LORD and still strong for war, he came to Joshua at Gilgal and asked for the hill country. Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron within Judah's portion. He drove out Anak's three sons, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, offered his daughter Achsah to whoever took Kiriath Sepher, and gave her upper and lower springs when she asked.

l: Levites, The Book of Joshua
s: The Levites are a tribe with no land inheritance, since their inheritance is the LORD's priesthood. Their family heads petition Eleazar, Joshua, and tribal heads at Shiloh, and per the LORD's command through Moses receive forty-eight pastured cities from Israel, divided among Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites.

l: children of Joseph, The Book of Joshua
s: The children of Joseph, also called the house of Joseph, are a group made up of two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim, living in the north. They first receive a lot with a border from the Jordan at Jericho through the hill country to the sea. They then complain to Joshua that a single allotment is too small for a numerous people blessed by the LORD. Joshua affirms their great power and promises them the hill country and victory over the Canaanites.

l: Manasseh, The Book of Joshua
s: Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn, is a tribal group: son Machir received Gilead and Bashan as a man of war, other families received lots, and ten parts fell west of the Jordan, yet its children failed to drive out Canaanites.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Joshua
s: possesses hill country of Ephraim [too narrow for the house of Joseph] Ephraim's territory lay south of Manasseh's along the brook of Kanah, and Ephraim held Tappuah on Manasseh's border and some cities among Manasseh's cities. Ephraim is named with Manasseh as the house of Joseph, whose hill country was said to be too narrow for them.

l: hill country (Hebron region), The Book of Joshua
s: was_inhabited_by Anakim [with great and fortified cities] Caleb asked Joshua for this hill country, which the LORD had spoken of at Kadesh Barnea. He noted that the Anakim and great fortified cities were there, and hoped to drive them out with the LORD's help.

l: cities of the Levites, The Book of Joshua
s: includes_feature pasture lands [around every city] The Levites hold forty-eight cities in all, each with its surrounding pasture lands. Five of them, Hebron, Shechem, Golan, Kedesh in Galilee, and Ramoth in Gilead, are named as cities of refuge for the man slayer.

l: Othniel the son of Kenaz, The Book of Joshua
s: Othniel, Caleb's brother, captured Kiriath Sepher (Debir) and was rewarded with Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife.

l: Achsah, The Book of Joshua
s: Achsah is Caleb's daughter, offered as wife to whoever captures Kiriath Sepher and given to Othniel after he takes it. Arriving, she prompts a field request, then asks Caleb for a blessing and water, and he gives her upper and lower springs.

l: Judah's allotment boundaries, The Book of Joshua
s: Judah's allotment is defined by four borders. The south border runs from the Salt Sea's bay through Edom's side, Zin, Kadesh Barnea and Azmon to the brook of Egypt and the sea. The east is the Salt Sea, the west the great sea, and the north runs from Beth Hoglah through Jerusalem-area valleys to Jabneel.

l: city lists of Judah, The Book of Joshua
s: A regional catalogue of Judah's cities, each group with its villages: twenty-nine in the South, then lowland groups (fourteen, sixteen, nine) plus Ekron, Ashdod and Gaza, then hill country groups (eleven, nine, ten, six, two), ending with six in the wilderness.

l: children of Ephraim, The Book of Joshua
s: The children of Ephraim received an inheritance with a defined border according to their families, from Ataroth Addar and upper Beth Horon to the Jordan and the sea. They also received cities with villages set apart within Manasseh's inheritance. They did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer.

l: inheritance of the children of Ephraim, The Book of Joshua
s: The territory allotted to the children of Ephraim by families. Its eastern border runs from Ataroth Addar to upper Beth Horon, then westward at Michmethath, around Taanath Shiloh, past Janoah, Ataroth, Naarah and Jericho to the Jordan. Another line runs from Tappuah along the brook of Kanah to the sea. It also includes set-apart cities within Manasseh's inheritance.

l: Shechem, The Book of Joshua
s: Shechem is a hill-country city in Ephraim, designated a city of refuge for the man slayer. Joshua gathers all the tribes there to make the covenant, and a great stone is set up under the oak. Joseph's bones are buried in the parcel Jacob bought from Hamor's sons, becoming Joseph's children's inheritance.

l: Zelophehad, The Book of Joshua
s: Zelophehad, son of Hepher in a lineage through Gilead, Machir and Manasseh, had no sons, only five daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.

l: daughters of Zelophehad, The Book of Joshua
s: receives inheritance allotment of Manasseh [inheritance among the brothers of their father, per the LORD's commandment] Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah came to Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the princes, citing the LORD's command to Moses that they receive an inheritance among their brothers. According to that command, Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father's brothers.

l: inheritance allotment of Manasseh, The Book of Joshua
s: Manasseh's inheritance allotment comprised Gilead and Bashan beyond the Jordan plus ten parts west of it, with Zelophehad's daughters receiving shares among their father's brothers. Gilead went to the remaining sons of Manasseh. The border ran from Asher to Michmethath before Shechem, down to the brook of Kanah, bounded by Ephraim south, Asher north, Issachar east, and the sea. It also held towns in Issachar and Asher: Beth Shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach, Megiddo.

l: Shiloh, The Book of Joshua
s: Shiloh is a place in Canaan where the congregation set up the Tent of Meeting, surveyors reported to Joshua at the camp, and Joshua cast lots before the LORD to divide remaining land.

l: tribe of Benjamin, The Book of Joshua
s: Tribe of Benjamin: received the first lot at Shiloh by families, its territory bordering Judah and the house of Joseph, and was allotted twenty-six cities with their villages.

l: seven tribes, The Book of Joshua
s: Seven tribes still lack their inheritance. Joshua urges them to stop delaying; their land is to be surveyed into seven portions and allotted by lot at Shiloh, while Judah stays south and Joseph's house north.

l: surveyors (men appointed from each tribe), The Book of Joshua
s: Three men from each tribe were appointed to walk through the land and describe it according to their inheritance. They went out, surveyed it by cities into seven portions in a book, and returned to Joshua at the camp at Shiloh.

l: casting of lots, The Book of Joshua
s: Joshua cast lots for the seven portions in Shiloh before the LORD to divide the land among the tribes. The first lot to come up was that of the tribe of Benjamin.

l: Benjamin's borders and territory, The Book of Joshua
s: Benjamin's territory is defined by its boundaries: a north border from the Jordan by Jericho through the hill country to Beth Aven, Bethel, and Ataroth Addar; the Jordan on the east; Kiriath Jearim ending the west; and a south border to the Salt Sea's north bay. Its cities include Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, Ramah, and Jerusalem, grouped in twelve and fourteen.

l: tribe of Simeon, The Book of Joshua
s: The tribe of Simeon received the second lot of the land, with its inheritance located in the middle of Judah's territory because Judah's portion was too large. It gained thirteen cities with villages, including Beersheba, Moladah, Ziklag and Sharuhen, plus four more cities and surrounding villages to Baalath Beer.

l: tribe of Zebulun, The Book of Joshua
s: The tribe of Zebulun received the third lot of the land, with a border from Sarid west to Maralah, then east through several towns to the valley of Iphtah El, and an inheritance of twelve cities with villages.

l: tribe of Issachar, The Book of Joshua
s: The tribe of Issachar received the fourth lot of land; its border ran through Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem, Tabor, Shahazumah and Beth Shemesh, ending at the Jordan, totaling sixteen cities with villages.

l: tribe of Asher, The Book of Joshua
s: The tribe of Asher received the fifth lot in the land distribution; its border ran from Helkath and Achshaph to Carmel, Zebulun, Sidon, Tyre and the sea, totaling twenty-two cities with villages.

l: Naphtali, The Book of Joshua
s: Naphtali is a tribal group whose territory is a land allotment. It received the sixth lot, with a border from Heleph to the Jordan and Hukkok, bounded by Zebulun, Asher and Judah, and held nineteen cities with villages, including fortified Ziddim, Hammath, Chinnereth and Hazor.

l: tribe of Dan, The Book of Joshua
s: The tribe of Dan received the seventh lot, including cities like Zorah, Eshtaol, Aijalon, Timnah and Ekron. Going beyond their border, they fought and took Leshem, settled there, and renamed it Dan after their forefather.

l: Leshem, The Book of Joshua
s: is_renamed Dan [after the conquest] Leshem was attacked by the children of Dan, who struck it with the edge of the sword, took it, possessed it and lived in it. They renamed it Dan after their forefather.

l: lot distribution of the land, The Book of Joshua
s: A lot distribution of the land, conducted by Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the heads of the fathers' houses at Shiloh before the LORD, at the Tent of Meeting's door. Lots fell in order to Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and Dan, completing the division.

l: cities of refuge (for the man slayer), The Book of Joshua
s: The cities of refuge are six designated places, previously commanded through Moses, where a person who kills unintentionally can flee from the avenger of blood. They are Kedesh in Naphtali, Shechem in Ephraim, Kiriath Arba (Hebron) in Judah, Bezer from Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead from Gad, and Golan in Bashan from Manasseh. They serve all the children of Israel and the alien living among them. Their elders hear the fugitive's case, take him in, and give him a place to live.

l: man slayer (unintentional killer), The Book of Joshua
s: A man slayer is a person who kills accidentally or unintentionally. He may flee to a city of refuge, declare his case to the elders at the gate, and receive a place to live. He dwells there until he stands before the congregation for judgment and the high priest dies, then returns to his own city and house.

l: avenger of blood, The Book of Joshua
s: may_not_receive man slayer (unintentional killer) [the city's elders must not deliver him up because he killed unintentionally and bore no prior hatred] The avenger of blood is the one from whom the cities of refuge give protection. If he pursues the man slayer, the city's people must not hand the man over to him, because the man struck his neighbor unintentionally and did not hate him before.

l: Kohathites, The Book of Joshua
s: receives_cities_count ten [rest of the children of Kohath, from Ephraim, Dan and half-tribe of Manasseh] The Kohathites receive the first lot, and their share totals twenty-three cities. The children of Aaron among them receive thirteen cities, and the rest of the Kohathites receive ten out of Ephraim, Dan, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

l: children of Aaron the priest, The Book of Joshua
s: Aaron's children, a Kohathite Levite family, receive the first lot in the Levite city allotment: thirteen cities from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin, including refuge city Hebron, whose fields and villages go to Caleb.

l: Gershonites, The Book of Joshua
s: receives_cities_count thirteen [from Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan] The Gershonites receive thirteen cities by lot out of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan. Golan in Bashan and Kedesh in Galilee are among them as cities of refuge.

l: Merarites, The Book of Joshua
s: receives_cities_count twelve [from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun] The Merarites, described as the rest of the Levites, receive twelve cities out of Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad. Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge, is among them.

l: Allotment of cities by lot, The Book of Joshua
s: is_commanded_by LORD [by Moses] The cities are distributed to the Levite families by lot, as the LORD commanded by Moses. The first lot falls to the Kohathite children of Aaron, followed by the rest of the Kohathites, the Gershonites, and the Merarites.

l: Phinehas, The Book of Joshua
s: Phinehas, a priest and son of Eleazar, holds a hill in Ephraim's hill country. He leads ten princes to Gilead to accuse the eastern tribes of rebellion, is satisfied by their explanation, affirms the LORD is among them, and reports back to Israel.

l: altar (built by Reuben, Gad and Manasseh), The Book of Joshua
s: A great altar built beside the Jordan in Canaan by Reuben, Gad and Manasseh. Israel, provoked, prepares for war, but the builders explain it is a copy of the LORD's altar, a witness between sides and generations, not for sacrifice, and name it "A Witness Between Us that the LORD is God."

l: nations (remaining among Israel), The Book of Joshua
s: The remaining nations are allotted to Israel as inheritance, and the LORD will drive them out if Israel stays faithful. Israel must not mingle with them or mention, swear by, serve, or bow to their gods; clinging to them would make them snares, traps, scourges, and thorns.

l: gods (of the nations), The Book of Joshua
s: were_served_by Terah [beyond the River] The gods served by the fathers beyond the River and in Egypt, and the gods of the Amorites, are named as the alternatives to the LORD. Joshua tells the people to put them away and warns that serving foreign gods will bring the LORD's judgment. The people reject them, saying far be it from them to forsake the LORD to serve other gods.

l: good land (Israel's land), The Book of Joshua
s: The land is described as good and as given by the LORD to Israel. Joshua warns that if Israel disobeys, they will perish quickly from off this good land. The land is thus the stake in Israel's obedience.

l: covenant of the LORD, The Book of Joshua
s: has_condition obedience [disobedience kindles the LORD's anger] The covenant is something the LORD commanded Israel. Joshua says that disobeying it by going to serve and bow down to other gods will kindle the LORD's anger and cause Israel to perish from the land.

l: intermarriage with the nations, The Book of Joshua
s: Intermarriage with the nations is forbidden to Israel. Joshua warns that clinging to the nations' remnant through marriage makes the LORD stop driving them out; they become a snare, trap, scourge and thorns until Israel perishes from the good land.

l: warning of destruction for disobedience, The Book of Joshua
s: A warning in Joshua's address (Chapter 23): as the LORD's promised good things came, so evil will follow if Israel breaks the covenant and serves other gods. His anger will kindle, and they will quickly perish from the good land.

l: covenant at Shechem, The Book of Joshua
s: is_between Joshua [Joshua and the people] Joshua makes a covenant with the people at Shechem after they promise to serve the LORD and listen to his voice, and he sets for them a statute and an ordinance. He records the words in the book of the law of God and sets up a great stone under the oak by the LORD's sanctuary as a witness against them, lest they deny their God.

l: The First Book of Kings
s: This document is the book of 1 Kings, tracing Israel's monarchy from David's death through Solomon's glory and the kingdom's division to the reign of Ahab and the prophet Elijah's ministry. It opens with a succession struggle: the aged David, after Nathan and Bathsheba intervene against Adonijah's self-proclaimed kingship, has Solomon anointed. Solomon then secures his throne, eliminating Adonijah, Joab and Shimei and removing Abiathar. At Gibeon he asks the LORD for an understanding heart, receives wisdom, riches and honor, and shows it in the judgment between two women claiming one child. Chapters 4 to 10 portray his reign: administrators, provisioning officers, wide dominion and peace. With Hiram of Tyre's timber and forced labor he builds the temple over seven years, then his own house, and the ark is installed amid the LORD's glory, followed by Solomon's prayer and a fourteen-day dedication feast. The LORD warns him to stay faithful; the queen of Sheba visits and his wealth grows immense. Chapter 11 turns the story: his many foreign wives lead him to worship other gods, the LORD announces the kingdom will be torn away, adversaries rise, and Ahijah tells Jeroboam he will receive ten tribes. Solomon dies, succeeded by Rehoboam. In chapter 12 Rehoboam rejects the people's plea to lighten the yoke, Israel rebels and makes Jeroboam king, and only Judah with Benjamin stays loyal. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan. A man of God confronts him, but is deceived by an old prophet and killed by a lion (ch. 13). Ahijah pronounces doom on Jeroboam's house when his son dies (ch. 14). Chapters 14 to 16 survey rulers of Judah and Israel in turn: Rehoboam, Abijam, and the reforming Asa in Judah; Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri and finally Ahab in Israel, with dynasties ended by murder. Ahab, married to Jezebel, serves Baal and does more evil than any predecessor. Chapters 17 to 19 center on Elijah: he announces drought, is fed by ravens and a widow, and revives her son. On Mount Carmel the LORD's fire defeats the prophets of Baal and rain returns. Fleeing Jezebel, Elijah meets the LORD at Horeb in a still small voice and is told to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha. The last chapters follow Ahab: he defeats Ben Hadad of Syria but spares him and is rebuked (ch. 20); he and Jezebel have Naboth killed for his vineyard, and Elijah foretells their fate (ch. 21). Ahab dies at Ramoth Gilead despite disguise, as Micaiah predicted, and the book ends with Jehoshaphat's reign and Ahaziah's evil rule over Israel (ch. 22).

l: David, The First Book of Kings
s: David is a king of Israel, a servant of the LORD who kept his commandments, and father of Solomon. He reigned forty years: seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. The records open with him old and unable to keep warm, unaware that Adonijah has made himself king. Moved by Bathsheba and Nathan, he fulfills his oath and has Solomon anointed at Gihon. Near death he charges Solomon to keep the LORD's law, to deal with Joab and Shimei, and to show kindness to Barzillai's sons. He dies and is buried in David's city, Jerusalem. Afterward he is remembered mainly through Solomon: wars prevented him from building the LORD's house, though it was in his heart, and the LORD promised his son would build it. Solomon asks that David never lack a man on Israel's throne. David becomes the standard of a wholehearted heart against which Solomon is judged. For David's sake the kingdom's tearing is delayed and one tribe is left, giving him a lamp in Jerusalem. His conquests in Edom and Zobah form the background to later adversaries.

l: Adonijah, The First Book of Kings
s: Adonijah, handsome son of King David and Haggith, born after Absalom, exalts himself as king with backing from Joab and Abiathar. When Solomon is anointed, his guests flee and he clings to the altar in fear. Solomon spares him conditionally, but after Adonijah asks for Abishag through Bathsheba, Solomon deems it a threat and has Benaiah kill him.

l: Joab, The First Book of Kings
s: Joab, son of Zeruiah and captain of the army, followed Adonijah rather than Absalom and killed Abner and Amasa in peacetime. David cites these killings; Joab flees to the altar, refuses to leave, is killed by Benaiah on Solomon's order, and is buried at home.

l: Abiathar, The First Book of Kings
s: Abiathar is a priest who bore the ark before David; Solomon, though judging him deserving of death, spares him, removes him from the priesthood and exiles him to his Anathoth fields, Zadok replacing him, fulfilling the word about Eli's house.

l: Benaiah, The First Book of Kings
s: Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, executes Solomon's orders to kill Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei, then replaces Joab as army commander over Israel.

l: Nathan, The First Book of Kings
s: Nathan, a prophet excluded from Adonijah's feast, advises Bathsheba, confirms her plea to David about his oath, and helps anoint Solomon king at Gihon.

l: Shimei, The First Book of Kings
s: Shimei, son of Gera from Bahurim, a Benjamite who cursed David. Sworn safe from the sword, he is confined to Jerusalem by Solomon; after three years he crosses to Gath for runaway slaves, breaking the oath, and Benaiah kills him.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon is a king of Israel, son of David and Bathsheba and younger brother of the elder Adonijah. The records follow him from accession to decline. In Chapter 1, David, recalling his oath, has Zadok anoint him at Gihon, the people proclaim him, and he sits on David's throne. In Chapter 2 he consolidates power: Adonijah, Joab and Shimei are killed, Abiathar is removed from the priesthood, Benaiah is set over the army and Zadok made priest, and he honors Bathsheba at his right hand. He allies with Pharaoh by marrying his daughter. He loves the LORD yet sacrifices at high places. At Gibeon he asks God for an understanding heart, receives unequaled wisdom, riches and honor, and shows his wisdom by judging the dispute of two women over a child. He rules all Israel through a list of named officers, holds dominion from the River to the Philistines and Egypt's border, receives tribute, enjoys peace on all sides, keeps forty thousand horse stalls and twelve thousand horsemen, and speaks three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs. With rest from enemies, he builds the LORD's house as promised to David. He gets cedar from Hiram of Tyre, raises forced labor levies and large crews of burden bearers and stone cutters, and finishes the temple in seven years. He then spends thirteen years on his own house, the House of the Forest of Lebanon, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter, makes the golden furnishings and deposits David's dedicated gifts. He brings the ark in, prays the dedicatory prayer and offers great sacrifices. The LORD appears again with a conditional promise and warning. He gives Hiram twenty cities, builds a fleet at Ezion Geber, receives the queen of Sheba, and builds an ivory and gold throne, gold shields and bucklers. He gathers 1,400 chariots and trades horses and chariots with Egypt, the Hittites and Syria, exceeding all earth's kings in riches and wisdom. The end turns bleak: he takes seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, who turn his heart in old age to Ashtoreth, Milcom, Chemosh and Molech, with high places built for them. His heart is not perfect with the LORD as David's was. The LORD raises adversaries, Hadad the Edomite and Rezon. He seeks to kill Jeroboam, reigns forty years, dies, is buried in the city of David, and his son Rehoboam succeeds him.

l: Bathsheba, The First Book of Kings
s: Bathsheba, mother of Solomon, is warned by Nathan of Adonijah's reign and the danger to her and Solomon. She reminds David of his oath, and he affirms it. Later she carries Adonijah's request for Abishag to Solomon, who honors her but refuses and condemns Adonijah.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings
s: Israel is a people, named from Jacob by the LORD, who is also treated as a land and later a northern kingdom. It begins in prosperity under Solomon: with Judah it is numerous as the sand by the sea, and lives safely from Dan to Beersheba, each man under his vine and fig tree. Its elders and tribes gather to feast and sacrifice before the ark, and Solomon prays for forgiveness when they sin and repent. Warnings follow that abandoning the LORD would cut it off from the land and make it a proverb and byword; it had also been told not to mingle with the nations whose women Solomon loved, and it suffered the adversary Rezon. The pivotal break comes at Shechem, where Israel asks Rehoboam for a lighter yoke, is refused, declares no portion in David, stones Adoram, rebels against David's house, and makes Jeroboam king. They follow his calf worship at Bethel and Dan. A prophecy declares Israel will be struck like a reed, uprooted from the good land, and scattered beyond the River for its Asherah poles and Jeroboam's sins. Kings follow in succession: Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri, Ahab, each following Jeroboam's sin, with war against Judah, attacks by Ben Hadad, and a contested kingship between Tibni and Omri. Under Ahab, the people gather at Mount Carmel, stay silent, then after the fire fall on their faces and declare the LORD is God; Elijah's twelve stones recall the tribes of Jacob. Mustered at seven thousand, Israel defeats the Syrians at Samaria and Aphek despite looking like two little flocks of goats. The record ends with Ahab's war for Ramoth Gilead, Micaiah's vision of Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd, the army dispersing after Ahab's death, and Ahaziah beginning to reign in Samaria.

l: Judah, The First Book of Kings
s: Judah is the southern kingdom, with Jerusalem as its capital, loyal to David's house. After Israel rebelled, Judah and Benjamin stayed with Rehoboam and turned back from war at the LORD's word. Judah then does evil in the LORD's sight, worse than its fathers, building high places, sacred pillars and Asherah poles, and harboring sodomites. In Rehoboam's fifth year Shishak of Egypt attacks Jerusalem and takes its treasures. Abijam rules three years, then Asa forty-one, followed by Jehoshaphat. Judah is at war with Israel and pressed by Baasha's building of Ramah, which Asa's call to all Judah dismantles.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings
s: The LORD is the God of Israel, also called God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, and titled God of Armies. He chooses Israel as a great, innumerable people, separates them as his inheritance, brought them out of Egypt, cast out the Amorites before them, and loves them forever. He chose David and Jerusalem, and makes holy the temple Solomon built, where he dwells in thick darkness and puts his name forever. He promises to dwell among Israel on condition of obedience. The records stress that his favor rests on obedience, and that his spoken word is reliably fulfilled. The account begins with Solomon. The LORD appears to him at Gibeon, grants wisdom, riches and honor, gives rest on every side, and fills the newly built house with glory in a cloud. Solomon says heaven cannot contain him. He appears a second time, promising to establish the throne if Solomon is faithful and warning of Israel being cut off if they serve other gods. The queen of Sheba says he set Solomon on the throne out of love for Israel, to do justice and righteousness. Then the turn. Angry that Solomon turned away, the LORD decrees the kingdom torn from his son, not in Solomon's days and leaving one tribe for David's and Jerusalem's sake. He raises adversaries, promises Jeroboam ten tribes, and brings about Rehoboam's refusal to listen so that his word through Ahijah stands. He forbids Judah and Benjamin to fight their brothers. He sends a man of God against Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, and judges the man's disobedience as well. Jeroboam's idolatry brings judgment on his house, while Abijam receives a lamp in Jerusalem for David's sake. In the northern kingdom, his word through prophets destroys the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, and his anger is provoked by successive kings, especially Ahab. He sustains Elijah with ravens and a widow, revives her child, and sends fire on Carmel so the people declare that the LORD is God. At Horeb he speaks after the still small voice, commissions Hazael, Jehu and Elisha, and reserves seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal. He gives Ahab victory over Syria, then condemns him for Naboth's murder, delaying the evil because Ahab humbled himself. Finally, enthroned among the army of heaven in Micaiah's vision, he accepts a lying spirit to entice Ahab to fall, and his word about the dogs is fulfilled.

l: succession to David's throne, The First Book of Kings
s: The succession is contested: Adonijah claims the throne with the backing of Joab and Abiathar, while David had sworn that Solomon would reign after him. David settles it by having Solomon anointed at Gihon and seated on the throne. Adonijah's supporters disperse, and Adonijah submits to Solomon.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of Kings
s: David reigns thirty-three years in Jerusalem, and Shimei is ordered to build a house and live there without leaving. Shimei lives there many days until his trip to Gath.

l: Gath, The First Book of Kings
s: Two of Shimei's slaves run away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. Shimei goes there and brings them back, and this trip breaks Solomon's restriction and leads to his death.

l: David’s charge to Solomon, The First Book of Kings
s: requires Law of Moses [keep the LORD's instruction] David urges Solomon to be strong, keep the LORD's law, and act wisely so that the promise of a man on the throne holds. He directs Solomon not to let Joab die in peace, to show kindness to Barzillai's sons, and to bring Shimei down to Sheol with blood. Solomon goes on to act on the instructions concerning Joab and Shimei.

l: house of the LORD (the temple Solomon built), The First Book of Kings
s: The house of the LORD is the temple built by Solomon in Jerusalem, called by the LORD's name and built to fulfill his word to David that his son would build it. It measured sixty cubits long, twenty wide and thirty high, with a porch, lattice windows and side rooms on three floors. It was built of stone prepared at the quarry, covered and lined with cedar, and overlaid with gold. What matters most is that it is the place where the LORD puts his name and presence. The account begins with preparations: timber from Hiram and costly worked stones, prepared by Solomon's builders, Hiram's builders and the Gebalites. The foundation was laid in Ziv of the fourth year and the work finished in Bul of the eleventh year. Hiram's bronze work, including the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the molten sea, bases and basins, was installed, along with gold furnishings and the things David dedicated. The ark was placed in the most holy place, a cloud and the LORD's glory filled the house, and Solomon and all Israel dedicated it with sacrifices. The LORD then declared it holy forever, but warned that if Israel turned away he would cast it out and it would become an object of astonishment.

l: Solomon's dream at Gibeon, The First Book of Kings
s: After Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon, the LORD appears to him by night in a dream and tells him to ask for what he should be given. The dream contains Solomon's request, God's gift of wisdom, riches and honor, and a conditional promise of long life. Solomon awakes and recognizes it was a dream.

l: Solomon's request for an understanding heart, The First Book of Kings
s: pleases LORD Solomon, calling himself a little child who does not know how to go out or come in, asks for an understanding heart to judge God's great people and discern good from evil. He passes over long life, riches, and the death of enemies. The request pleases the LORD.

l: ark of the LORD's covenant, The First Book of Kings
s: The ark of the LORD's covenant is a sacred object carried by priests from David's city, Zion, and placed in the inner sanctuary beneath the cherubim's wings. Its poles are visible only from the holy place, and it holds solely the two stone tablets Moses placed at Horeb.

l: first woman (the living child's mother), The First Book of Kings
s: A prostitute and mother of the living child. She says the other woman took her son at midnight and left a dead child; when the king orders the child divided, she pleads to give him away to save him, and is declared the mother.

l: other woman (mother of the dead child), The First Book of Kings
s: A prostitute whose child died at night when she lay on it; accused of switching babies, she claims the living child, then demands its division at the king's order, losing it to the first woman.

l: living child, The First Book of Kings
s: The living child is claimed by both women and is ordered by the king to be divided in two with a sword. He is spared when the first woman pleads for his life, and the king gives him to her as his mother.

l: dead child, The First Book of Kings
s: The dead child died in the night when his mother lay on him. According to the first woman, he was placed in her bosom in place of her living son, and she recognized in the morning that he was not hers.

l: Solomon's judgment, The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon's judgment: he orders a living child divided by sword between two women; their opposite reactions reveal the true mother, who receives the child. All Israel hears, sees God's wisdom in him, and fears the king.

l: wisdom of God, The First Book of Kings
s: The wisdom of God is what the people of Israel see in Solomon after his judgment, and it is understood as enabling him to do justice. It reflects the wise and understanding heart the LORD gave him in answer to his request.

l: twelve officers (Solomon's officers), The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon's twelve officers are a group with authority over all Israel, each assigned a district and responsible for supplying food to the king and his household for one month of the year. They are listed with their districts, from Ben Hur in Ephraim's hill country and Ahimaaz in Naphtali to Geber the son of Uri in Gilead, the only officer in that land. Two of them, Ben Abinadab and Ahimaaz, are married to Solomon's daughters. They also provision everyone at Solomon's table, letting nothing be lacking, and bring barley and straw for the horses.

l: Ahijah the Shilonite, The First Book of Kings
s: Ahijah is a prophet of the LORD and his servant, living in Shiloh. He tore a garment into twelve pieces, giving Jeroboam ten, to foretell the kingdom's division from Solomon's house. Later, blind with age, he is warned by the LORD, recognizes Jeroboam's disguised wife, and pronounces judgment on Jeroboam's house and Israel; his word is fulfilled.

l: Ramoth Gilead, The First Book of Kings
s: is_held_by Syria [claimed by Israel] Ahab claims Ramoth Gilead as Israel's and complains that it remains in the hand of the king of Syria. Ahab and Jehoshaphat go up to it to fight, and the battle there ends with Ahab's death.

l: Lebanon, The First Book of Kings
s: Lebanon is the place where cedar trees are to be cut for Solomon's building project, with Solomon's servants working alongside Hiram's. Hiram's servants bring the timber down from Lebanon to the sea. Solomon sent his levy there in shifts of ten thousand men per month, one month in Lebanon and two at home.

l: Solomon's daily provision, The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon's daily provision is a large food supply: thirty cors of fine flour, sixty measures of meal, thirty fat and pasture cattle, one hundred sheep, plus deer, gazelles, roebucks and fattened fowl, supplied month by month by twelve officers.

l: Solomon's wisdom, The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon's wisdom is a gift from God, put in his heart, with abundant understanding and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore. It surpasses the wisdom of the children of the east, of Egypt, and of Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Darda. Chapter 4 shows its scope: three thousand proverbs, one thousand five songs, and knowledge of trees, animals, birds, creeping things, and fish. Its fame spreads among surrounding nations, and kings send people to hear him. In Chapter 10 the queen of Sheba tests him, finds nothing hidden from him, and says the reality exceeds the report. All the earth seeks him, and he exceeds all kings in wisdom.

l: Hiram, The First Book of Kings
s: Hiram is the king of Tyre who had always loved David. On hearing of Solomon's anointing he sent servants, blessed the LORD for David's wise son, and agreed to supply cedar and cypress timber floated down from Lebanon, receiving yearly wheat and oil and making a treaty. Later he furnished cedar, cypress and gold, received twenty Galilean cities, disliked them, calling them Cabul, yet sent 120 talents of gold and experienced sailors for Solomon's Ophir fleet.

l: cedar and cypress timber, The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon requests cedar from Lebanon, and Hiram agrees to provide cedar and cypress timber according to all Solomon's desire. It is to be brought down to the sea, made into rafts, floated to the place Solomon specifies, and broken up there for him to receive. Hiram gave the timber, and in exchange Solomon supplied wheat and oil for Hiram's household.

l: levy of forced laborers (Solomon's levy), The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon's levy was thirty thousand forced laborers drawn from all Israel, supervised by Adoniram. They worked in rotation of ten thousand monthly in Lebanon, one month there and two at home, alongside seventy thousand burden bearers, eighty thousand stone cutters, and 3,300 officers.

l: inner sanctuary (the LORD's house), The First Book of Kings
s: The inner sanctuary, the most holy place at the back of the house, is a twenty-cubit cube prepared to hold the ark of the LORD's covenant. Built of cedar and overlaid with pure gold, it is fronted with gold chains and entered through carved, gold-overlaid olive-wood doors.

l: cherubim (inner sanctuary), The First Book of Kings
s: Two cherubim of olive wood, made by Solomon for the inner sanctuary, each ten cubits high with five-cubit wings spanning ten cubits, identical in measure and form. Overlaid with gold, their wings touch both walls and each other mid-house, covering the ark.

l: gold, The First Book of Kings
s: Gold was used to overlay the whole house within, including the inner sanctuary in pure gold, the altar belonging to the inner sanctuary, the floor, and the cherubim. Solomon also drew chains of gold before the inner sanctuary and overlaid the carved doors with gold fitted on the engraved work.

l: cedar, The First Book of Kings
s: Cedar was used for the beams and planks covering the house, the timbers on which the side-room floors rested, and the boards lining the walls from floor to ceiling. The interior cedar was carved with buds and open flowers so that no stone was visible. Cedar was also used for the back part of the house forming the inner sanctuary, for the altar's covering, and for a course of beams in the inner court.

l: construction of the temple, The First Book of Kings
s: The temple's construction began in Ziv of Solomon's fourth year, 480 years after Israel left Egypt. Stone was pre-cut at the quarry so no iron tool was heard on site, and work finished in Bul of the eleventh year, after seven years.

l: Hiram, The First Book of Kings
s: Hiram is a skilled bronze worker brought from Tyre by King Solomon, son of a Naphtali widow and a Tyrian bronze-working father. Filled with wisdom, understanding and skill, he made the two pillars, molten sea, ten bases and basins, pots and shovels, finishing all his work for Solomon in the LORD's house.

l: bronze pillars (Jachin and Boaz), The First Book of Kings
s: Two bronze pillars made by Hiram, each eighteen cubits high and twelve in circumference, topped with five-cubit molten bronze capitals decorated with nets, chains, pomegranates and lilies; set at the temple porch, right named Jachin, left Boaz.

l: molten sea, The First Book of Kings
s: The molten sea is a large basin, ten cubits brim to brim, five cubits high, thirty cubits around, with a lily-like brim, holding two thousand baths. It rests on twelve oxen, three facing each of four directions, and is placed on the house's right side, eastward toward the south.

l: ten bronze bases, The First Book of Kings
s: Ten identical bronze bases made by Hiram, each four cubits long and wide and three high, cast in one casting, measure, and form. Panels show lions, oxen, and cherubim; four bronze wheels like chariot wheels support each. Each carried a forty-bath basin, and five stood on each side of the house.

l: golden vessels and furnishings of the LORD's house, The First Book of Kings
s: Golden vessels and furnishings made by Solomon for the LORD's house, all of pure gold. They begin with the altar and show-bread table, then ten lamp stands, five per side before the inner sanctuary, plus flowers, lamps, tongs, cups, basins, spoons, fire pans, and door hinges.

l: Solomon's prayer, The First Book of Kings
s: is_a prayer of dedication [supplication for Israel and the foreigner] Solomon praises the LORD as incomparable and covenant-keeping, then asks him to hear and forgive when people pray toward the house in cases of oath-swearing, defeat, drought, famine, pestilence, war, and exile. He also asks that the LORD answer the foreigner's prayer so all peoples may know his name. It ends with Solomon rising from kneeling and blessing the assembly.

l: dedication feast, The First Book of Kings
s: A fourteen-day dedication feast held in Ethanim, the seventh month, before the LORD. Solomon and all Israel, from Hamath's entrance to Egypt's brook, attend; he offers 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep as peace offerings, then dismisses the blessing people on the eighth day.

l: Horeb, The First Book of Kings
s: Horeb, called God's Mountain, is the site of the LORD's covenant with Israel and has a cave; Elijah arrives after forty days, camps there, and the LORD passes by.

l: twenty cities in Galilee (Cabul), The First Book of Kings
s: is_called the land of Cabul [named by Hiram, displeased] Solomon gives these twenty cities in the land of Galilee to Hiram after twenty years of building. Hiram visits them, is displeased, and calls them the land of Cabul, a name that remains to this day.

l: forced labor, The First Book of Kings
s: Forced labor is Solomon's conscripted workforce for building the LORD's house, his own house, Millo, Jerusalem's wall, Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer, plus storage and chariot cities. It was levied from surviving Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, not Israelites, overseen by 550 chief officers.

l: God's conditional promise and warning to Solomon, The First Book of Kings
s: God's conditional covenant with Solomon: if he walks in integrity and uprightness like David and keeps the statutes, his throne over Israel will be established forever. If he or his children turn to other gods, Israel will be cut off from the land, the house cast out, and passersby will explain it as abandoning the LORD.

l: queen of Sheba, The First Book of Kings
s: The queen of Sheba travels to Jerusalem with a great caravan to test Solomon with hard questions. Overwhelmed by all she sees, she says not half was told her, praises the LORD, gives Solomon gold, spices and precious stones, receives all she desired, and returns home.

l: Solomon's wealth, The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon's wealth is a topic of extraordinary riches. It begins with 666 talents of gold yearly, excluding trade and tribute, then lists gold shields, an ivory throne overlaid with gold, and gold vessels. Silver became as common as stones in Jerusalem, the Tarshish fleet brought luxuries, and he surpassed all earth's kings.

l: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, The First Book of Kings
s: Jeroboam the son of Nebat was an Ephraimite from Zeredah, son of Nebat and a widowed mother, Zeruah. A mighty man of valor, he served Solomon, who put him in charge of the labor of the house of Joseph. Ahijah promised him ten tribes and a sure house if he walked in the LORD's ways. After he lifted his hand against the king and Solomon sought to kill him, he fled to Shishak in Egypt until Solomon died. Recalled, he spoke for the assembly to Rehoboam and was made king over all Israel. He built Shechem and Penuel, then, fearing the people would return to Rehoboam, made two golden calves for Bethel and Dan, appointed non-Levite priests of the high places, and devised a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month. At the Bethel altar he ordered a man of God seized and his hand dried up, restored only through the man's intercession; he offered a meal and reward, which was refused, yet did not turn from his evil way. When his son Abijah fell sick, he sent his wife in disguise to Ahijah, and was condemned for doing evil above all before him, making other gods and molten images. He reigned twenty-two years and was continually at war with Rehoboam, and war continued with Abijam. His son Nadab succeeded him, but his house was cut off, destroyed by Baasha according to the LORD's word through Ahijah. His sin, by which he made Israel sin, became the standard for later kings.

l: Hadad the Edomite, The First Book of Kings
s: Hadad, an Edomite royal offspring, fled to Egypt as a child after Joab struck Edom's males. Favored by Pharaoh, he married Tahpenes's sister and fathered Genubath. Hearing David and Joab were dead, he sought to return home, and the LORD raised him as Solomon's adversary.

l: Rezon the son of Eliada, The First Book of Kings
s: Rezon, son of Eliada, fled his lord Hadadezer of Zobah, gathered a troop as captain, settled in Damascus, and was raised by God as Solomon's adversary, abhorring Israel and reigning over Syria.

l: Rehoboam, The First Book of Kings
s: Rehoboam, son of Solomon and Naamah the Ammonitess, became king of Judah at forty-one and reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem. At Shechem he rejected the old men's counsel and answered Israel roughly, losing the northern tribes; he fled to Jerusalem after Adoram was stoned. He heeded the LORD through Shemaiah and did not fight Israel. Shishak took the treasures, so he replaced gold shields with bronze. Continually at war with Jeroboam, he was buried in David's city, succeeded by his son Abijam.

l: Solomon's foreign wives, The First Book of Kings
s: Solomon's foreign wives, from Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, Hittite peoples and Pharaoh's daughter, turned his aging heart to other gods; he built high places, and they burned incense and sacrificed.

l: the kingdom, The First Book of Kings
s: is_divided_into twelve parts [ten tribes to Jeroboam, one to Solomon's son] The LORD declares he will tear the kingdom from Solomon, but not in his days; it will be torn from his son's hand, with one tribe left for David's and Jerusalem's sake. Ahijah's twelve-piece garment symbolizes the split, with ten tribes going to Jeroboam.

l: Solomon's idolatry and its punishment, The First Book of Kings
s: has_punishment kingdom torn from Solomon's line [ten tribes given to Jeroboam] Solomon followed Ashtoreth, Milcom, Chemosh, and Molech and built high places for his wives' gods, doing evil in the LORD's sight. The punishment is the loss of the kingdom's ten tribes from his son's hand, along with the adversaries Hadad and Rezon and the rise of Jeroboam, with mercy shown for David's sake.

l: old men (Solomon's counselors), The First Book of Kings
s: Elders who had stood before Solomon during his life advised Rehoboam to serve the people and answer kindly so they would serve him forever; Rehoboam abandoned their counsel.

l: young men (Rehoboam's companions), The First Book of Kings
s: Young men who grew up with Rehoboam stood before him and advised harshness: claiming his little finger was thicker than his father's waist and adding to the yoke. Rehoboam followed their counsel, speaking those words to the people.

l: yoke (Solomon's burden on Israel), The First Book of Kings
s: is_a heavy burden [hard service imposed by Solomon] The people called Solomon's yoke and hard service difficult and asked Rehoboam to lighten it in exchange for their service. Rehoboam instead promised to add to it, which triggered Israel's rebellion.

l: golden calves, The First Book of Kings
s: Two golden calves made by Jeroboam, declared the gods who brought Israel out of Egypt, were placed in Bethel and Dan; the text condemns this as sin as people traveled to worship.

l: Bethel, The First Book of Kings
s: Bethel is a place where Jeroboam set a golden calf, built an altar, installed high-place priests, and sacrificed and burned incense at a feast. It then becomes the site of the man of God's prophecy against that altar, home of the old prophet, and the prophecy extends to high-place houses across Samaria's cities.

l: altar (at Bethel), The First Book of Kings
s: The altar at Bethel is where Jeroboam burned incense; a man of God cried against it, prophesying Josiah would sacrifice high-place priests there, and as the fulfilled sign it splits apart, ashes poured out.

l: division of the kingdom, The First Book of Kings
s: is_a rebellion of Israel against David's house The kingdom divided when Israel rejected Rehoboam and David's house, making Jeroboam king, while only Judah (with Benjamin) stayed with Rehoboam. The text presents it as brought about by the LORD, who told Judah not to fight to reverse it.

l: man of God (from Judah), The First Book of Kings
s: A prophetic messenger from Judah, sent by the LORD to Bethel, who prophesied against the altar, gave a sign, and healed Jeroboam's hand. Forbidden to eat, drink, or return the same way, he refused the king's food but was deceived by an old prophet's lie and ate. A lion killed him on the road; he was buried in the old prophet's grave.

l: old prophet (of Bethel), The First Book of Kings
s: An old prophet living in Bethel, father of sons and owner of a donkey. He rode after the man of God and deceived him, claiming an angel's command, to bring him home to eat. At the table the LORD's word brought judgment through him. After the lion's attack he buried the body in his own grave, mourned him, and affirmed the prophecy.

l: lion, The First Book of Kings
s: A lion in Chapter 13 meets the disobedient man of God from Judah on the road and kills him as judgment, then stands by the body and donkey without eating or mauling them, which passersby take as the LORD's word fulfilled.

l: Samaria, The First Book of Kings
s: Samaria is a hill that Omri buys from Shemer for two talents of silver, builds on, and names after Shemer. Omri is buried there, and Ahab reigns from there and raises an altar for Baal in the house of Baal he built in Samaria. Samaria is the city Ben Hadad besieges and where Ahab consults the elders. Ben Hadad's father had made streets in Samaria, and Ahab returns there sullen and angry at the end.

l: commandment against eating and drinking in Bethel, The First Book of Kings
s: The LORD's command forbade the man of God from Judah to eat, drink, or return the way he came in Bethel. He kept it before the king, yielded to the old prophet's lie, and was condemned to die by a lion.

l: house of Jeroboam, The First Book of Kings
s: has_fate utterly swept away [judgment decreed by the LORD] The house of Jeroboam is condemned to be cut off and swept away like dung, with those who die in the city eaten by dogs and those in the field by birds. Only Abijah will come to the grave. A king raised up by the LORD will cut the house off, and Nadab succeeds Jeroboam as king.

l: Jeroboam's wife, The First Book of Kings
s: is_married_to Jeroboam Jeroboam's wife disguises herself and travels to Shiloh with ten loaves, cakes, and a jar of honey. Ahijah recognizes her by the sound of her feet and gives her heavy news. She returns to Tirzah, and the child dies as she reaches the threshold of the house.

l: Abijah, The First Book of Kings
s: Abijah, Jeroboam's son, falls sick, leading his father to seek Ahijah's word. Because some good toward the LORD was found in him, he alone of Jeroboam's house receives burial and mourning; he dies as his mother enters the city, and all Israel mourns.

l: Tirzah, The First Book of Kings
s: Tirzah is the royal city where Baasha is buried and where Elah reigns and is killed in Arza's house. Zimri reigns there seven days, Omri besieges it, and Zimri burns the king's house there. Omri reigns six years in Tirzah before moving to Samaria.

l: Nadab, The First Book of Kings
s: Nadab, son of Jeroboam, became king of Israel in Asa's second year and reigned two years, doing evil by following his father's sin. While besieging Gibbethon, he was conspired against and killed by Baasha, who took his throne.

l: Abijam, The First Book of Kings
s: Abijam was king of Judah who reigned three years in Jerusalem, son of Maacah. His heart was not perfect with the LORD, unlike David, as he walked in his father's sins. He warred with Jeroboam, yet for David's sake received a son. He died, was buried in David's city, and Asa succeeded him.

l: Abijah's death and burial, The First Book of Kings
s: Abijah, Jeroboam's son, dies at Tirzah as his mother reaches the house threshold, fulfilling Ahijah's word; all Israel buries and mourns him, and he alone of his house receives a grave because of some good found in him.

l: Ahijah's prophecy against Jeroboam's house, The First Book of Kings
s: A prophecy Ahijah delivers from the LORD to Jeroboam's wife for Jeroboam: it charges idolatry despite his exaltation, then foretells his house swept away like dung, the child's death, a king ending the dynasty, and Israel scattered beyond the River; fulfillment begins with the child's burial and Jeroboam's death.

l: Asa, The First Book of Kings
s: Asa was king of Judah, reigning forty-one years in Jerusalem. Son of Maacah's line, he did right in the LORD's eyes like David, and his heart stayed perfect with the LORD all his days. He removed idols and deposed Maacah for making an abominable image, though he left the high places. Constantly at war with Baasha, he secured a treaty with Ben Hadad and used Ramah's stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah. In old age his feet were diseased. He was buried in Jerusalem, succeeded by his son Jehoshaphat.

l: Baasha, The First Book of Kings
s: Baasha, of the house of Issachar, was a king of Israel. He conspired against Nadab, killed him at Gibbethon in Asa's third year, and reigned twenty-four years from Tirzah. He destroyed Jeroboam's whole house, fulfilling the LORD's word, yet walked in Jeroboam's evil way. He fought Asa, built Ramah, then withdrew to Tirzah when Ben Hadad attacked. The LORD condemned him through Jehu. He was buried in Tirzah, succeeded by his son Elah.

l: Ben Hadad, The First Book of Kings
s: Ben Hadad, son of Tabrimmon, was king of Syria and lived at Damascus. Hired by Asa, he broke his treaty with Baasha and struck Israelite towns and Naphtali. Later he besieged Samaria with thirty-two allied kings, demanded Ahab's wealth and family, and was routed while drunk. He returned at Aphek, was defeated, fled, and was spared by Ahab, promising to restore cities and give streets in Damascus.

l: Jehoshaphat, The First Book of Kings
s: Jehoshaphat, son of Asa and Azubah, was king of Judah, reigning twenty-five years in Jerusalem from the fourth year of Ahab. He did right like Asa and made peace with Israel. He joined Ahab at Ramoth Gilead, insisting on a prophet of the LORD, and was spared when mistaken for Ahab. He lost his ships at Ezion Geber, then died and was buried in David's city, succeeded by Jehoram.

l: Ramah, The First Book of Kings
s: was_built_by Baasha [to blockade Asa; building stopped] Baasha built Ramah to keep anyone from going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah. When Ben Hadad attacked Israel, Baasha stopped building it. Asa had all Judah carry away its stones and timber and used them to build Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah.

l: war between Asa and Baasha, The First Book of Kings
s: lasts all their days The text states twice that there was war between Asa and Baasha all their days. It included Baasha's building of Ramah to blockade Judah, Asa's payment to Ben Hadad of Syria to break his treaty with Baasha, and Ben Hadad's attack on Israelite cities. The result was that Baasha abandoned Ramah and Asa took its materials.

l: Jehu the son of Hanani, The First Book of Kings
s: is_a prophet Jehu the son of Hanani, called a prophet, receives and delivers the LORD's word against Baasha and his house. The prophecy foretells that Baasha's house will be swept away like the house of Jeroboam, and it is later fulfilled.

l: house of Baasha, The First Book of Kings
s: The house of Baasha is prophesied to be swept away, with its dead eaten by dogs in the city and birds in the field. Zimri fulfills this by killing all of Baasha's house, leaving no male relative or friend, because of the sins of Baasha and Elah.

l: Elah, The First Book of Kings
s: Elah, son of Baasha, reigns over Israel in Tirzah for two years, then is killed by his servant Zimri while drunk in Arza's house.

l: Zimri, The First Book of Kings
s: Zimri, a chariot captain serving Elah, kills the king in Tirzah and seizes the throne, destroys Baasha's house, but reigns only seven days before burning the palace over himself when Omri besieges Tirzah.

l: Omri, The First Book of Kings
s: Omri, army captain, is made king by Israel in the camp at Gibbethon, besieges Tirzah and ends Zimri's reign, then overcomes Tibni's faction. He reigns twelve years, buys and builds Samaria, does evil above all before him in Jeroboam's way, dies and is buried in Samaria; Ahab succeeds him.

l: Ahab, The First Book of Kings
s: Ahab, son of Omri, is king of Israel who reigns twenty-two years from Samaria, where he is buried. He marries Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal, serves and worships Baal, builds a house and altar for Baal in Samaria, and makes the Asherah, doing more evil than any earlier king and provoking the LORD. He also builds an ivory house and cities. In the records he first appears sending Obadiah to find grass for his horses and mules during famine, and searching for Elijah, whom he calls a troubler of Israel; Elijah answers that Ahab and his father's house forsook the LORD's commandments, and the contest at Mount Carmel follows. Against Ben Hadad he wins two victories after prophetic words, but calls him brother, makes a covenant, and lets him go; a prophet says his life will replace Ben Hadad's, and he goes home sullen and angry. He then covets Naboth's vineyard and lets Jezebel arrange Naboth's death. Confronted by Elijah, he tears his clothes and fasts in sackcloth, so the LORD delays the evil to his son's day. Finally he hates and imprisons Micaiah for prophesying evil, disguises himself in battle at Ramoth Gilead, is struck by a random arrow, and dies at evening. His son Ahaziah succeeds him.

l: Jezebel, The First Book of Kings
s: Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal and wife of Ahab king of Samaria, is a domineering figure who incites Ahab to evil and cuts off the LORD's prophets.
