She threatens Elijah through a messenger after hearing of the prophets' killing, then arranges Naboth's false trial and stoning to seize his vineyard. The LORD foretells her fate: dogs will eat her by the rampart of Jezreel.

l: Baal, The First Book of Kings
s: Baal is the god the people are urged to follow if he is God, and Ahab and his father's house are said to have followed the Baals. When his prophets call on him from morning until evening, there is no voice, no answer, and nobody paying attention. Elijah mocks that he may be deep in thought, away, on a journey, or asleep.

l: conspiracy of Zimri against Elah, The First Book of Kings
s: Zimri, captain of half of Elah's chariots, conspires against his master and kills him in Tirzah while Elah is drunk in Arza's house. It fulfills the LORD's word against Baasha's house, but when the army at Gibbethon hears of it they make Omri king, and Zimri's reign ends in seven days.

l: Elijah the Tishbite, The First Book of Kings
s: Elijah the Tishbite is a settler of Gilead, a prophet and servant of the LORD, before whom he stands, with the LORD's word in his mouth. The widow calls him a man of God. He opens by telling Ahab no dew or rain will fall except by his word, then obeys the LORD's commands to live by the brook Cherith and in Zarephath, where he promises the widow that her meal and oil will not run out and prays her dead son back to life. On Mount Carmel he challenges the people to choose between the LORD and Baal, sees the LORD's fire fall, and has the prophets of Baal killed at the brook Kishon. He prays for rain and, with the LORD's hand on him, runs ahead of Ahab to Jezreel. Jezebel, his enemy, threatens his life, so he flees to Beersheba and the wilderness, asks to die, is fed by an angel, and at Horeb twice says he alone is left and jealous for the LORD. He is told to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha, and puts his mantle on Elisha, who follows and succeeds him. He later confronts Ahab in Naboth's vineyard, announcing judgment on Ahab, his house, and Jezebel.

l: Zarephath, The First Book of Kings
s: belongs_to Sidon Zarephath is a city belonging to Sidon, to which the LORD sends Elijah after the brook dries up. Its gate is where Elijah meets the widow gathering sticks, and it is where he stays in her house.

l: widow (of Zarephath), The First Book of Kings
s: The widow is found gathering sticks at the city gate and says she has only a handful of meal and a little oil, intending to bake a last meal for herself and her son before they die. She obeys Elijah, makes him a cake first, and her household eats for many days. When her son dies she accuses Elijah of bringing her sin to memory, but after he is revived she says she knows he is a man of God and that the LORD's word in his mouth is truth.

l: son (the widow's son), The First Book of Kings
s: The widow's son becomes so sick that no breath is left in him. Elijah takes him from his mother's bosom, lays him on his own bed upstairs, and prays over him, and the child's soul comes back into him and he revives. Elijah then hands him back to his mother, saying he lives.

l: drought (no dew nor rain), The First Book of Kings
s: Elijah announces to Ahab that there will be no dew or rain for these years except according to his word. The effects appear when the brook Cherith dries up because there is no rain in the land. The LORD's promise to the widow that her jars will not fail lasts until the day he sends rain on the earth.

l: jar of meal, The First Book of Kings
s: has_state does not run out [until the LORD sends rain] The widow has only a handful of meal in a jar, which she plans to bake for herself and her son. After Elijah promises in the LORD's name that it will not run out, it does not run out, according to the LORD's word spoken by Elijah.

l: jar of oil, The First Book of Kings
s: has_state does not fail [until the LORD sends rain] The widow has a little oil in a jar, which she plans to use with the last of her meal. Elijah promises that it will not fail until the LORD sends rain, and it does not fail, according to the LORD's word spoken by Elijah.

l: resurrection of the widow's son, The First Book of Kings
s: A miracle in which the LORD answers Elijah's prayer in the upper room: after the widow's son stops breathing, Elijah stretches over him three times, the child revives, and his mother, receiving him back, affirms Elijah is a man of God.

l: Obadiah, The First Book of Kings
s: Obadiah is a man who runs Ahab's household and has feared the LORD greatly since youth. He hid one hundred prophets in caves, fifty each, feeding them during Jezebel's purge. Afraid Ahab will kill him, he nonetheless tells Ahab of Elijah after Elijah swears to appear.

l: prophets of Baal (Baal), The First Book of Kings
s: A group of 450 prophets of Baal, gathered at Mount Carmel alongside Asherah prophets fed at Jezebel's table. They call on Baal all day, leaping and cutting themselves, without answer; after the LORD's fire falls, Elijah has them seized and killed at Kishon.

l: Mount Carmel, The First Book of Kings
s: Mount Carmel is where Ahab gathers all Israel and the prophets of Baal and of the Asherah at Elijah's demand. It is the site of the contest and the fire from the LORD. Afterward Elijah goes up to its top to bow down and pray for rain.

l: contest on Mount Carmel, The First Book of Kings
s: A contest on Mount Carmel where Elijah proposes the God who answers by fire is God. Baal's prophets call all day without answer; Elijah's soaked altar is consumed by the LORD's fire, and the people acknowledge the LORD as God.

l: altar of the LORD, The First Book of Kings
s: The LORD's thrown-down altar is repaired by Elijah with twelve stones, then trenched, loaded with wood and a cut bull, and drenched with water three times; the LORD's fire consumes offering, wood, stones, and dust.

l: fire from the LORD, The First Book of Kings
s: consumed altar of the LORD [burnt offering, wood, stones, dust, and water] After Elijah's prayer at the evening offering, the LORD's fire falls and consumes the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licks up the water in the trench. It leads the people to fall on their faces and declare that the LORD is God.

l: rain, The First Book of Kings
s: promised_by LORD [to fall on the earth in the third year] The LORD promises to send rain on the earth in the third year of famine. After the contest Elijah tells Ahab he hears the sound of abundance of rain, and his servant on the seventh look sees a small cloud like a man's hand rising from the sea. Soon the sky grows black with clouds and wind and a great rain falls.

l: Elisha, The First Book of Kings
s: Elisha, son of Shaphat from Abel Meholah, is a landowner plowing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah casts his mantle on him. He asks to bid his parents farewell, slaughters the oxen and feeds the people, then leaves to follow and serve Elijah.

l: angel (the LORD's angel), The First Book of Kings
s: provides food (cake and water for Elijah) [to Elijah] The LORD's angel touches Elijah as he sleeps under the juniper tree and tells him to arise and eat, and a cake baked on the coals and a jar of water are at his head. The angel comes a second time, saying the journey is too great for him, and Elijah goes in the strength of that food.

l: wind, earthquake, and fire (theophany at Horeb), The First Book of Kings
s: As the LORD passes by, a great and strong wind tears the mountains and breaks rocks in pieces, then an earthquake comes, then a fire passes. The text states that the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire.

l: still small voice, The First Book of Kings
s: follows fire After the fire, there is a still small voice. When Elijah hears it, he wraps his face in his mantle, goes out, and stands in the entrance of the cave, where a voice asks him what he is doing there.

l: mantle (Elijah's mantle), The First Book of Kings
s: Elijah wraps his face in his mantle when he hears the still small voice. Later he puts his mantle on Elisha as he passes him plowing, after which Elisha leaves the oxen and runs after him.

l: Syrians, The First Book of Kings
s: The Syrians are a group who mistakenly believe the LORD is only a god of the hills. After fleeing Israel at Samaria, they regroup on the plain at Aphek, where huge numbers die and a wall falls. Later, at peace with Israel, they hold Ramoth Gilead; a Syrian archer's random shot strikes Ahab.

l: Aphek, The First Book of Kings
s: is_a city [had a wall] Aphek is where Ben Hadad musters the Syrians to fight Israel at the return of the year. After the defeat the survivors flee into its city, where a wall falls on twenty-seven thousand men and Ben Hadad hides in an inner room.

l: prophet (who spoke to Ahab), The First Book of Kings
s: A prophet tells Ahab the LORD will deliver the great multitude, names the young men of the princes of the provinces as the means, and says Ahab should begin the battle. He later warns Ahab to strengthen himself because the king of Syria will return at the year's end. A man of God then gives the word before Aphek.

l: young men of the princes of the provinces, The First Book of Kings
s: has_count two hundred and thirty-two These young men, two hundred and thirty-two in number, are named by the LORD as the means of victory and go out first at noon. Each kills his man, and the Syrians flee.

l: prophet (son of the prophets who disguised himself), The First Book of Kings
s: is_a son of the prophets This prophet asks a fellow to strike him; the first refuses and is killed by a lion, and the second strikes and wounds him. He disguises himself with a headband over his eyes, tells Ahab a story about a lost prisoner so that Ahab pronounces his own judgment, then reveals himself and announces the LORD's sentence on Ahab.

l: siege of Samaria, The First Book of Kings
s: targets Samaria Ben Hadad and thirty-two kings besiege Samaria and send demands that Ahab give up silver, gold, wives, and children, plus a search of the houses. After Ahab refuses the second demand, the Syrians prepare to attack, but Israel sallies out at noon and routs them, and Ben Hadad escapes on a horse.

l: battle at Aphek, The First Book of Kings
s: Battle at Aphek ends in Israel's victory: after seven days encamped, Israel kills one hundred thousand Syrian footmen in a day; survivors flee into Aphek, a wall kills twenty-seven thousand, and Ben Hadad begs for life.

l: covenant between Ahab and Ben Hadad, The First Book of Kings
s: A covenant between Ahab and Ben Hadad: after servants plead for Ben Hadad's life, Ahab calls him brother and spares him; Ben Hadad restores his father's seized cities and grants Damascus streets, but a prophet condemns the release.

l: Naboth the Jezreelite, The First Book of Kings
s: Naboth the Jezreelite owns an ancestral vineyard beside Ahab's palace in Jezreel; he refuses to surrender it, is falsely accused of cursing God and the king, and is stoned to death.

l: vineyard (Naboth's vineyard), The First Book of Kings
s: Naboth's vineyard in Jezreel, beside Ahab's palace, is coveted by Ahab as a herb garden; Naboth refuses, dies, Ahab takes possession, and Elijah confronts him there.

l: elders and nobles (of Naboth's city), The First Book of Kings
s: live_in Naboth the Jezreelite [lived with Naboth in his city] The elders and nobles who lived with Naboth receive Jezebel's letters and do exactly as instructed, proclaiming a fast and setting Naboth on high among the people. They carry out the false trial and stoning and then send word to Jezebel that Naboth is dead.

l: wicked fellows (false witnesses against Naboth), The First Book of Kings
s: testifies_against Naboth the Jezreelite [falsely claimed he cursed God and the king] Two wicked fellows are set before Naboth at Jezebel's direction. In the presence of the people they testify falsely that Naboth cursed God and the king, which leads to his stoning.

l: Naboth's stoning, The First Book of Kings
s: Naboth the Jezreelite is stoned outside the city on false testimony arranged by Jezebel's letters; she then tells Ahab to seize the vineyard, prompting the LORD's judgment through Elijah.

l: Judgment against Ahab's house, The First Book of Kings
s: A divine judgment decreed by the LORD through Elijah: evil will come on Ahab, his male descendants will be swept away, and his house will match those of Jeroboam and Baasha. Dogs will devour Jezebel and Ahab's line, but Ahab's humbling postpones the evil to his son's day.

l: Micaiah the son of Imlah, The First Book of Kings
s: Micaiah, son of Imlah, is a prophet of the LORD whom Ahab hates for prophesying evil. Asked by Jehoshaphat, he first echoes others, then truthfully foretells Israel's scattering and the lying spirit; he is struck, jailed, and stakes his prophecy on Ahab's fate.

l: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah, The First Book of Kings
s: Zedekiah, a prophet foretelling victory, makes iron horns and predicts the king will crush the Syrians; he strikes and mocks Micaiah, who warns Zedekiah will hide in an inner room.

l: prophets of Ahab, The First Book of Kings
s: About four hundred prophets gathered by Ahab unanimously tell him to attack Ramoth Gilead and prosper, but Micaiah reveals the LORD put a lying spirit in their mouths to entice Ahab.

l: lying spirit (sent by the LORD to entice Ahab), The First Book of Kings
s: In Micaiah's vision a spirit comes before the LORD and offers to entice Ahab by being a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. The LORD says it will entice him and prevail, and tells it to go out and do so.

l: battle at Ramoth Gilead, The First Book of Kings
s: Ahab and Jehoshaphat fight at Ramoth Gilead, with Ahab in disguise and Jehoshaphat in his robes. The Syrian chariot captains pursue Jehoshaphat until they see he is not the king of Israel, then a random arrow wounds Ahab. The battle increases that day, and at sunset a cry goes out for every man to return to his city and country.

l: Ahab's death, The First Book of Kings
s: Ahab's death: struck by an arrow between his armor's joints, he is propped in his chariot facing the Syrians until he dies at evening. He is buried in Samaria; dogs lick his blood at the washed chariot's pool, fulfilling the LORD's word.

l: Ahaziah the son of Ahab, The First Book of Kings
s: Ahaziah, son of Ahab, asks Jehoshaphat to let his servants sail together but is refused. He reigns over Israel in Samaria two years, doing evil like his father, mother and Jeroboam, and serving Baal.

l: The Second Book of Kings
s: The Second Book of Kings (chapters 1-25) is a narrative history of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, tracing both from the aftermath of Ahab's death to the fall of Jerusalem and exile in Babylon. Its central figures are the prophets Elijah and Elisha, a long line of kings, and the LORD, whose word repeatedly proves true. The opening chapters center on prophecy. Elijah pronounces death on Ahaziah of Israel, calls down fire, and is taken up by a whirlwind, and Elisha takes his mantle and double portion of spirit. Elisha then works many miracles: healing water, multiplying oil, raising the Shunammite's son, healing Naaman of leprosy, floating an ax head, and blinding a Syrian army. He also prophesies victory over Moab and relief from the Syrian siege of Samaria. His servant Gehazi is struck with leprosy for greed. Elisha's word brings Hazael to the Syrian throne and prompts the anointing of Jehu. Jehu kills Joram, Ahaziah of Judah, and Jezebel, whom dogs eat as Elijah had said. He then destroys Ahab's house and the worshipers of Baal, yet keeps the sins of Jeroboam. In Judah, Athaliah seizes power until the priest Jehoiada crowns the hidden child Joash; Joash later repairs the temple but pays tribute to Hazael and is assassinated. Elisha dies, and a dead man revives on touching his bones. Israel's kings then follow in swift, violent succession, with Assyria intruding. Hoshea's rebellion leads Assyria to take Samaria and deport Israel, which the text blames on idolatry and ignored prophets. Judah survives longer. Hezekiah trusts the LORD, and when Sennacherib's envoy Rabshakeh threatens Jerusalem, Isaiah promises deliverance and an angel strikes 185,000 Assyrians. Hezekiah is healed and given fifteen more years, but Isaiah rebukes him for showing Babylon's envoys his treasures and foretells Babylonian conquest. Manasseh's grave evil seals Judah's fate. Josiah finds the book of the law, makes a covenant, purges idolatry, and keeps Passover, yet the LORD's wrath stays because of Manasseh. Josiah is killed by Pharaoh Necoh. His successors do evil, and Nebuchadnezzar subjugates Judah, deports Jehoiachin and many others, and installs Zedekiah. Zedekiah rebels, Jerusalem falls, the temple is burned, Zedekiah is blinded and taken to Babylon, and the governor Gedaliah is murdered, after which people flee to Egypt. The book ends with a small note of grace: Evilmerodach releases Jehoiachin from prison and honors him.

l: Elijah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Elijah is a hairy man in a leather belt, called a man of God and proven so by fire from the sky. Sent by the LORD's angel, he tells Ahaziah's messengers the king will die for consulting Baal Zebub. He calls fire on two captains of fifty and their men, spares a third who begs, and delivers the message to the king in person. He then travels with Elisha to the Jordan, parts it with his mantle, and is taken up to heaven by a whirlwind.

l: Ahaziah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ahaziah was a king of Israel in Samaria, also recorded as king of Judah. He fell through the lattice of his upper room and became sick, then sent messengers to Baal Zebub to ask whether he would recover. He sent three captains with fifty men each to Elijah; two companies were consumed by fire. Elijah told him he would not leave his bed. He died as the LORD said, and Jehoram succeeded him because he had no son.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings
s: The LORD is the God of Israel, the living God enthroned above the cherubim, creator of heaven and earth, called the Holy One of Israel, and, in Hezekiah's prayer, God alone of all earthly kingdoms. He appears throughout The Second Book of Kings as the sovereign who speaks through prophets, his servants Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah and Huldah, and whose word is repeatedly fulfilled. He has servants in Moses, David and Elijah. What matters most is his covenant relationship with Israel and Judah: he brought Israel out of Egypt, made covenant with Jacob's children, commands them to fear only him, and responds to obedience and idolatry with blessing or judgment. The account unfolds first in the prophetic era. He directs Elijah against King Ahaziah's messengers and takes Elijah up by a whirlwind. Through Elisha he divides the Jordan, heals waters, promises water and victory over Moab, answers prayer for a dead child, opens eyes to the fiery host, blinds and then restores the Syrians, and routs the Syrian army by the sound of chariots. He calls a famine and shows Hazael will rule Syria. He refuses to destroy Judah for David's sake, promising David a lamp always. Next he anoints Jehu to strike Ahab's house, fulfilling Elijah's words, and promises Jehu's sons the throne to the fourth generation, later fulfilled in Zechariah. Yet he begins cutting away parts of Israel through Hazael. In anger he delivers Israel to Syria but, gracious because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, gives a savior. He strikes Azariah with leprosy. Because of idolatry he removes the northern kingdom from his sight, and sends lions among settlers who did not fear him. With Hezekiah, who trusted and obeyed him, he is present and prospering him. He answers Hezekiah's prayer, strikes the Assyrian camp through his angel, heals Hezekiah, adds fifteen years, and defends Jerusalem for his own and David's sake, though he foretells Babylon carrying off the house's goods. Finally, provoked by Manasseh, he announces disaster on Jerusalem, which he had chosen for his name. He hears Josiah's humility but will not turn from wrath. He sends Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites, and removes Judah from his sight.

l: the LORD's angel, The Second Book of Kings
s: belongs_to LORD The LORD's angel goes out in the night and strikes 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. By morning they are all dead bodies.

l: Baal Zebub, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_a god of Ekron Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, is the one Ahaziah sends messengers to ask about his recovery. This is the reason the LORD pronounces death on the king, since it implies there is no God in Israel to inquire of.

l: Ahaziah's messengers, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ahaziah's messengers are sent to inquire of Baal Zebub but are met by Elijah and told to return to the king with the LORD's message of death. They return and report to the king, describing the man who met them as hairy and wearing a leather belt, which leads Ahaziah to identify him as Elijah the Tishbite.

l: fire from the sky (Elijah's call), The Second Book of Kings
s: Elijah calls fire down from the sky, on the condition that he is a man of God, and it consumes the first captain of fifty and his men. It does the same to a second captain and his fifty. The third captain refers to these events when he begs for his life and the lives of his fifty, and no fire falls on them.

l: Moab, The Second Book of Kings
s: Moab is a land that rebelled against Israel after Ahab's death, mustered its men at the border, mistook red water for blood, was routed while plundering, and was devastated, leaving only Kir Hareseth's stones.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings
s: Israel is both a people and a kingdom/land, with Samaria as its capital where kings reigned and an Asherah remained. It is portrayed as the people the LORD brought out of Egypt and for whom he cast out nations, yet it was torn from David's house and repeatedly sinned. Early on it appears as a land of witness: a captive Israelite girl, the prophet Elisha, and Naaman's conclusion that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Under Jehoram it marched with Judah and Edom against Moab, devastating the land before returning home. Syria attacked it, though Elisha's warnings protected it, and Samaria later endured siege and severe famine. Jehu purged Baal worship, but Israel kept the sins of Jeroboam, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and the LORD began cutting away its territory as Hazael struck east of the Jordan. Under Hazael and Benhadad it was oppressed, left to Jehoahaz with only fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, yet was given a savior because of the LORD's covenant. Jehoash recovered cities and defeated Judah at Beth Shemesh, plundering Jerusalem; under Jeroboam the LORD saw its bitter affliction with no helper and saved it rather than blot out its name, restoring borders. Decline followed: rapid succession of kings, Menahem's tribute to Assyria, and Tiglath Pileser's capture of northern lands. Ultimately Israel was carried to Assyria, settled in Halah, on the Habor and in the Medes' cities, because it feared other gods, worshiped Baal and the sky's army, built high places, made calves and an Asherah, passed children through fire, and ignored every prophet. The LORD removed it from his sight, leaving only Judah, and Ahab is later cited as a model of idolatry.

l: Ahab, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ahab is a ruler whose house is doomed by the LORD for the blood of Naboth and his sons. He has seventy sons in Samaria. Jehu destroys his whole house, cutting off every male, fulfilling Elijah's word and echoing the fates of Jeroboam's and Baasha's houses.

l: Samaria, The Second Book of Kings
s: Samaria is a city and capital of Israel under Hoshea. It appears first in Elisha's account, where a blinded Syrian army is led in and fed, then Benhadad besieges it and famine follows until Elisha's prophecy of cheap flour and barley is fulfilled. It holds Ahab's seventy sons, and Jehu kills Ahab's remnant there and is buried there. Finally Assyria besieges and captures it in Hoshea's ninth year and settles foreigners there.

l: Joram, The Second Book of Kings
s: Joram is a king of Israel, son of Ahab and Jezebel. He defended Ramoth Gilead against Hazael of Syria and was wounded, returning to Jezreel to heal, where Ahaziah visited. Confronted by Jehu, he fled crying treason, was killed by an arrow through the heart, and was thrown onto Naboth's plot.
